solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Rest — then time to visit church perfect for one in the country (13)

indicators.note: T drops in on the letters that follow, going inside them

blocks.note: to lie = to rest
surface padding: it only says the next piece follows
CH = church
the perfect is one example of a verb tense
T = time, placed inside CHTENSE to make CHTENS(T)E
the word itself, tacked on the end

explanation.surface: A traveller's itinerary: a rest, then a visit to a perfect church somewhere in the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perfect for one' is grammar, not praise: the perfect is a tense. 'In' looks like a link word but supplies the last two letters, leaving 'the country' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Liechtenstein is a small country between Switzerland and Austria.

clue.text: Lower profile, perhaps, to disappoint friends? (3,3,4,4)

blocks.note: read literally: let (allow) the side (profile) move down
the idiom for failing your team or companions

explanation.surface: Someone wondering whether keeping a low profile would disappoint their friends.
explanation.walkthrough: The first reading takes the idiom word by word: a side, or profile, being lowered. The question mark flags that playful literalism.
explanation.definitionFit: To let the side down is to fail the people relying on you.

clue.text: Praise from number of former partners outspoken? (5)

indicators.note: spoken out loud, so we go by sound

blocks.note: EX = former partner; a toll is a number, as in death toll

explanation.surface: Someone boasting candidly about how many exes they have had.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' looks like a count to be converted into a digit, but it is TOLL, a tally, as in body count or death toll.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both verbs mean to speak highly of someone.

clue.text: Type of profit which farmer makes in advance, incurring large fine (4-6)

definitions.note: an adjective: a half-yearly profit is one type of profit

indicators.note: HAY takes on, and so contains, the large fine

blocks.note: farmers make hay (while the sun shines)
L = large, as on clothing labels
F = fine, as on pencils
early = in advance

explanation.surface: A farmer who plans ahead but ends up paying a big fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Which farmer makes' points to the proverb about making hay while the sun shines. The answer is an adjective, so 'Type of profit' means a kind of profit, such as one reported every six months.
explanation.definitionFit: Profits are often reported half-yearly, every six months.

clue.text: Little use raising a single glass after wasting fifty years! (7)

indicators.note: in a down clue, raising lifts the word so it reads upwards, reversed
losing, so the letter for fifty goes
Y is placed after what remains

blocks.note: a monocle is a single eyeglass; raised it reads ELCONOM
L = fifty in Roman numerals, removed from ELCONOM to leave ECONOM
Y = years

explanation.surface: A toast raised by someone who has frittered away fifty years of their life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising a single glass' reads as drinking a toast, but the glass is a monocle, and raising it turns it upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: Economy is careful, sparing use of resources.

clue.text: Enamoured of one’s child, eating his food? (5,2)

blocks.note: infatuated with, in informal English
a literal picture: where a small child's dinner ends up when he eats messily

explanation.surface: A doting parent watching their child tuck into a meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a playful literal reading: the food is stuck on the child, which is what the question mark signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stuck on someone means being smitten with them.

clue.text: My outdated suggestion if looking for publicity? (4)

blocks.note: e.g. = for example, offering a suggestion
an ad is what you take out when looking for publicity

explanation.surface: Someone offering a dated piece of advice about getting noticed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My' is the exclamation, as in 'Oh my!', and 'outdated' says the answer is an old-fashioned one. Together E.G. AD reads as 'for example, an advert', exactly what you would suggest.
explanation.definitionFit: Egad is an archaic mild oath, like 'my!' or 'goodness'.

clue.text: What’s made by no one on stage, but just outside, so very loud? (6,3)

definitions.text: What’s made by no one on stage, but just outside, so very loud?

indicators.note: take only the outside letters of the word before

blocks.note: the word itself
I = one
the outside letters of STAGE
the word itself
ff = fortissimo, very loud in music

explanation.surface: A riddle about sounds produced in the wings of a theatre rather than on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: noises off are sounds made offstage, by no actor in view. At the same time it spells the answer word by word.
explanation.definitionFit: Noises off are stage effects heard from offstage.

clue.text: Town to keep golfing equipment? No, not surprisingly cutting it (8-2-4)

indicators.note: the letters come out in an unexpected order
the jumbled letters cut into IT, the golfing equipment

blocks.note: to stock goods is to keep them
tees hold the ball up for the drive
the letters to be rearranged, as ONONT, and set after the first T of TEES

explanation.surface: A town deciding whether to store golf gear, then flatly refusing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'It' points back to the golfing equipment, TEES, which gets cut open. Stockton-on-Tees is a town in north-east England.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockton-on-Tees is a market town in County Durham, England.

clue.text: Small child taking almost everything off (5)

indicators.note: not quite all of the word: its last letter is dropped
a child taking something holds it close, so TOT picks up AL and it joins on right after

blocks.note: a tot is a small child
ALL without its last letter

explanation.surface: A toddler stripping off all their clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Taking everything off' reads as undressing, but 'off' stands alone as the definition in its slang sense of kill or destroy.
explanation.definitionFit: To off and to total are both slang for kill or wreck.

clue.text: One making eyes at Louis dancing with Rex and Charlie (9)

indicators.note: dancers swap places across the floor, so the letters of AT LOUIS, R and C change their positions

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged
R = Rex, king
C = Charlie in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone flirting with Louis on the dance floor while Rex and Charlie look on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Making eyes at' reads as flirting, but 'at' belongs to the letters being rearranged. An ocularist literally makes eyes: artificial ones.
explanation.definitionFit: An ocularist is a specialist who makes artificial eyes.

clue.text: Completely ignored by wife, pledges flowers (10)

indicators.note: W (wife) is left out of the word

blocks.note: WHOLLY without W = wife
to hock something is to pawn, or pledge, it

explanation.surface: A wife who completely disregards her partner's promises and gifts of flowers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pledges' looks like promises, but here it is pawning: HOCKS.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the hollyhock is one kind of tall cottage-garden bloom.

clue.text: Soldier hired car (4)

blocks.note: short for mercenary
short for Mercedes

explanation.surface: A soldier who has rented a car.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface splits after 'Soldier', but the first definition is 'Soldier hired', a mercenary.
explanation.definitionFit: Merc is short for both mercenary and Mercedes.

clue.text: Wish lesson somehow could impart such wisdom (10)

indicators.note: the letters are put together in some other way

blocks.note: letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A hope that a lesson might somehow pass on wisdom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Such wisdom' points back to the kind of wisdom a lesson might give: the owl is the traditional symbol of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Owlishness is a solemn, wise look or manner, like an owl's.

clue.text: In need of oil to be so clean? (7)

blocks.note: describes a dry hinge that makes a high-pitched noise
completes an idiom: the word that goes before 'clean' to mean spotless

explanation.surface: A puzzled question about whether something must lack oil to count as truly clean.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition completes a phrase: squeaky clean, which is 'so' clean.
explanation.definitionFit: Squeaky means making a squeaking noise, and squeaky clean is spotless.

clue.text: Close to you, bear holding tongue? Apparently not! (9)

definitions.note: the definition points back to 'holding tongue': a person ululating is certainly not holding their tongue

indicators.note: the close, or last letter, of the word
LUG holds the next piece inside it

blocks.note: last letter of YOU
to lug is to carry, or bear
a tongue is a language

explanation.surface: A bear with its mouth shut, or perhaps not.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Apparently not!' refers back to 'holding tongue': someone ululating, howling or wailing, is anything but quiet. The bear is not an animal but the verb to carry.
explanation.definitionFit: Ululating means wailing loudly, the opposite of holding one's tongue.

clue.text: Poet in unfamiliar bar (7)

blocks.note: new = unfamiliar
to bar a door is to bolt it

explanation.surface: A poet sitting in a pub he doesn't know.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, but it is the fastening on a door. Sir Henry Newbolt was an English poet, best known for 'Drake's Drum'.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Sir Henry Newbolt (1862-1938) wrote patriotic verse such as 'Vitaï Lampada'.

clue.text: Shots not unique in assassination (7)

blocks.note: double measures of spirits
look at the spelling of ASSASSINATION: its Ss never stand alone but come in pairs

explanation.surface: An assassination in which more than one shot was fired.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half is a joke about spelling: in ASSASSINATION the Ss are not single but come as doubles.
explanation.definitionFit: Doubles are double measures of spirits, shots at the bar.

clue.text: Sinister trail pursued by Yankee (7)

indicators.note: Y comes after, following on behind

blocks.note: to shadow someone is to trail them
Y = Yankee in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: An ominous pursuit with an American on someone's tail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trail' is a verb, to follow someone secretly, not a path.
explanation.definitionFit: Shadowy means dark and sinister, working unseen.

clue.text: Case for subtenant providing flat for firm (7)

definitions.note: firm as a verb, to firm up

indicators.note: the case of a word is its outside letters

blocks.note: the outer letters of SUBTENANT
providing = if
a fen is flat marshland

explanation.surface: A legal argument that a subtenant should be given a flat by a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flat' is not a home but flat land, and 'firm' is the verb, not a company.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym, with firm as a verb: to make or become rigid.

clue.text: Bird from which to get down? (7)

blocks.note: the migratory bird
to get food down the throat, a verb

explanation.surface: A question about which bird to pluck for down feathers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' suggests feathers, but 'get down' means to swallow food.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: a fork-tailed migratory bird by example, and a plain verb synonym for gulping food past the throat.

clue.text: Lottery that’s without a winner? (4)

blocks.note: a raffle, where tickets are pulled from a hat
a match that ends level, a tie

explanation.surface: A lottery nobody wins.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a rollover; the second meaning is a tied match.
explanation.definitionFit: A draw is both a lottery and a game that nobody wins.

clue.text: A thousand thanks for organisation protecting a Zulu land (10)

indicators.note: the letters are to be organised afresh
the rearranged letters wrap round AZ

blocks.note: the word itself, part of the rearranged letters
K = a thousand
the word itself, part of the rearranged letters
the word itself, placed inside
Z = Zulu in the NATO alphabet

explanation.surface: Grateful words to a charity working to safeguard a Zulu homeland.
explanation.walkthrough: A K THANKS rearranges to K…AKHSTAN, which is split after its first letter to hold AZ.
explanation.definitionFit: Kazakhstan is a large country in Central Asia.

clue.text: What has no members — originally thirty, approximately (5)

indicators.note: take the origin, the first letter

blocks.note: first letter of THIRTY
or so = approximately

explanation.surface: A club reporting that its membership has fallen to nothing, having once been about thirty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' are limbs here, not people in a club: a torso is the body with no arms or legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A torso is the trunk of the body without its limbs.

clue.text: Voice of host, clear, periodically rising (4)

indicators.note: take letters at regular intervals
in a down clue, reading upwards reverses the letters

blocks.note: the even letters of HOSTCLEAR: o, t, l, a

explanation.surface: A presenter speaking clearly, with his voice going up at intervals.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters come out as OTLA and then read upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Alto is a singing voice, the lowest female range.

clue.text: Will and Henry messing with poor Eddy (9)

indicators.note: the letters are messed about

blocks.note: the word itself
H = henry, the unit of inductance
the word itself

explanation.surface: Two men, Will and Henry, bullying a hapless man called Eddy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eddy' sits at the end dressed as a man's name alongside Will and Henry, but it is the swirl of water.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: both name water spinning in a circular current.

clue.text: Where Eagles Dare? Not All Their Yesterdays, on reflection (5)

indicators.note: only part of the next words is used
reflected, so read backwards

blocks.note: sitting inside thEIR YEsterdays

explanation.surface: A list of film titles: Where Eagles Dare and Not All Their Yesterdays.
explanation.walkthrough: Where Eagles Dare is a war film, but read literally it describes an eagle's nest, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyrie is an eagle's nest, where eagles dare to live.

clue.text: One very virtuous, sporting pair? (5,3-5)

blocks.note: a smugly virtuous person
read literally: someone wearing, or sporting, two shoes

explanation.surface: A virtuous person and their sporting partner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sporting' suggests athletics, but here it means wearing, and the pair is a pair of shoes.
explanation.definitionFit: An idiom from an 18th-century nursery tale, for a smugly well-behaved person; read literally, it is anyone wearing both shoes.
